title: Chapter 2: Nine Souls on the Cable
content: By eight in the morning the landing looks like a church supper without the food.

Wren has been awake since five on Saturday morning and she has not changed her shirt. There is a wet line on the gravel where the water stopped, and above it, on the apron chain, somebody has tied a bunch of gladiolus from the Pyle garden with baler twine.

The town comes down the ramp in ones and twos. Ruthie Pyle first, with a thermos and a folding chair she does not sit in. Then the Methodist minister, in a golf shirt, because nobody called him before seven. Then Della Fenn's mother, who holds Wren's hand for a long time and says thank you twice and cannot look at the river. Then the Legion men, who put the flag at half mast at nine and are asked to raise it again at nine forty by a young man from the county, because there is no record of a death, and a flag at half mast is a record.
They raise it. Wren watches them do it. Nobody argues.
The word does not get said. That is the thing she notices before she notices anything else. Forty people on the landing and not one of them says drowned.

They say the water came up. They say the gate let go. They say he went in. They say we lost Elias, which is a sentence with no subject and no verb that means anything. Della Fenn says it was a flood and her mother says Della, and Della says well it was, and her mother says the county will call it what the county calls it.
Wren stands by the winch with her hands in her pockets and lets them talk.

At nine thirty the man in the clean jacket comes back down the ramp with a different clipboard. He has a name tag now. It says G. HALLORAN, FIELD TECHNICIAN, and there is a blue sticker on the board that says DISTRICT 4. He is fifty or so, with a mustache and a sunburn on the back of his neck, and the particular patience of a man who has been sent out to do a job nobody in the office wanted.
He does not introduce himself to the crowd. He comes to her.
"Ms. Aubrey. I'm sorry for your loss." He says it like a line he has said before, which it is. "I need a statement for the incident file."
"Write it yourself. You were standing there."
"I need it in your words."
She looks at the board. There is a form on it. There is a box at the top for the number of persons involved.
"How many passengers did you have aboard?"
"Nine."
He looks at his paper. "The preliminary has five."

"Then the preliminary is wrong." She takes him to the wheelhouse and opens the green book on the bench and turns it so the light falls on the page. Twelve September. Nine forty-four. Nine souls. Then the names, in her hand, in ink that has had all night to dry. "Della Fenn. Curtis Rudd. Denny Rudd. Porter Vail. Nessa Vail. June Pettit. Arlen Sample. Ida Quill. Tobe Quill. Tobe is eleven. He was sitting where you see that smudge."
He copies the names. His pen moves fast and small. She watches him write them and feels something she is not proud of, which is satisfaction.
"Can I take the book?" he says.
"No."
"It would help the file."
"It's not yours. It's not the county's. It stays in the wheelhouse."
He looks at her for a moment, and there is a flicker in his face that she cannot read, and then it is gone. "All right. For now."
"For always."
He writes something down. Then he asks her to describe the release.
"There was no siren."
"The gate ran a maintenance release," he says. "Silt management. Not a flood event. That's the classification."
"The water came up six feet in a minute and a half."
"That's what the release does. It's designed to scour the channel." He says scour like it is a good word. "The classification matters for the file. A maintenance release is not a flood."
"Then what is it?"
"It's an event."
"An event," she says. "My grandfather is an event."
He stops writing. For a second he looks like a man standing in cold water. Then he says, "I'm sorry," again, and it is worse the second time.

He goes up the ramp. The Legion flag is at the top of the pole now, and the wind has it straight out, and it is a beautiful morning, and the river is at the second rung again as if nothing has ever happened at Mile 9 in the whole history of the world.

Wren stays in the wheelhouse with the book open on the bench. His jacket is on the peg by the door, canvas, one elbow worn through to the lining, and it smells like diesel and tobacco and the inside of a coat. She does not touch it. She closes the book and puts it under the bench and pulls the tarp over it.
Mars arrives at eleven with two coffees and a folder she should not have.

Marisol Okonjo is twenty-six and works in the county records office two towns over, and she is the only person Wren has ever told anything true to. She hands over the coffee, looks at Wren's shirt, and does not say a word about it.
"There's no certificate," Mars says.
"I know there's no certificate."

"There's no certificate because there's no cause. The coroner's office won't put a cause on a man who was in the water forty minutes without a piece of paper from the Authority saying what the water was doing." She opens the folder. "And the Authority won't say what the water was doing until it finishes its own incident file. And the incident file needs a statement from the next of kin."
"Which is me."
"Which is you." Mars drinks her coffee. "They built it in a circle on purpose, Wren. It's not a mistake. A circle is cheaper than a decision."
At noon Wren walks up to the diner because Ruthie will not stop telephoning.

The Bend Diner has twelve stools and six tables and a pie case with a crack across one corner, and every seat is full of people who are not eating. Ruthie is behind the register with her school notebook open, writing, because Ruthie Pyle has kept a ledger since 1989 of who said what in her diner, and she says it is the only honest history this town has.
Hollis Drane is at the end of the counter with a slice of buttermilk pie he has not touched.

Hollis is sixty-one and has been the town clerk at the Annex for thirty years, and he has the face of a man who has spent three decades saying no to people he has to see at the grocery store. He is not a bad man. That is the problem with him.
"Sit down, Wren," he says. "Eat something."
"I'm not hungry."
"Eat something anyway. It's a long piece of road."
She sits. Ruthie puts a plate in front of her without asking, eggs and toast, and Wren eats two bites because it is easier than arguing.
"You'll want to file," Hollis says.
"File what?"
"Form 9." He says it the way a man says the name of a medicine. "Certificate of Loss. Four pages, triplicate. It's what the county uses when the death happens in a place the county doesn't own."
"The river."

"The river." He turns his cup around on the saucer. "Page one is the decedent. Page two is when and where. Page three is the informant, that's you. Page four is the office. Section six is the one that matters. Section six says cause, as certified."
"As certified by who?"

"By the district registrar. Which is the Basin Authority, District 4, on account of the death occurred in a release corridor." He says the words corridor and release the way other men say weather. "So you bring the form to the Annex, and the clerk takes it, and it goes to the district, and the district certifies, and then the county can write a certificate."
"And then?"

"And then there's a record. And then there's a burial permit, and an estate, and the little bit of money the state gives when a man dies in a public works event, if they call it that." He looks at his pie. "Without it there's nothing. He's not dead on paper. He's just not on paper."
Ruthie's pen stops moving.
"How long do I have?" Wren says.

Hollis does not want to answer. He answers anyway, because he is a clerk and a clerk cannot leave a question about a deadline alone. "The county holds remains seventy days. After that, if there's no certificate, they bury at Crown Hill at county expense and they close the file."
"Seventy days from when?"
"From the night he died." He counts on the counter with one finger, quietly, the way he counts everything. "That's the twenty-first of November."
Wren does the arithmetic in her head and does not like the answer. Seventy days is not a long time. Seventy days is a season.
"Will they certify it?" she says. "If I fill it out right. If I put the truth."

Hollis looks at her, and for a moment he is not a clerk at all. He is a man who has watched this happen before and has never once been able to stop it. "The district certifies what the district's file says. And right now the district's file says maintenance release."
"It says nine souls on a boat."
"It says nine souls on a boat," he agrees, "which is not a cause of death."

He gets up and puts three dollars on the counter, which Ruthie will not take, and she takes it anyway because he will not leave it. At the door he stops with his hand on the frame, and he does not turn around.
"One more thing," he says. "The ferry's policy lapsed in June."
Wren sets her fork down. "That's not possible. The county requires coverage to run a crossing."

"It is possible. The premium went up and the notice went to your grandfather and the notice went in a drawer." He is still not looking at her. "So there's no money in this. Not for the boat, not for you, not for anything. I'm telling you so you don't find it out in a bank."
The bell over the door goes off when he leaves.
Ruthie writes it down. Wren watches her write it, and then Ruthie closes the notebook and puts both hands flat on the counter and says, "Well. That's a hell of a thing to say on a Sunday."

Outside, the sun is on the water, and the ferry sits at the east ramp with her apron down and her cable slack, and Wren can see, from the diner window, the exact place on the chain where somebody tied the flowers.
highlight: The town gathers at the landing, and Hollis Drane explains that no stamp means no certificate and no burial.
